questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall it was a messy start-up, constant contradictions from UV, lack of information, lack of any help. Once we got going, it went ok. The exams and their silly scoring was messy. Changes came just before the exam (1 min before we started), during the exam or after. It seemed like there wasn't a standard for grading, but each teacher made up what was required. The exam itself was chaotic, in addition to the changes, these include: missing photocopies, unprintable photocopies, silence during the exam (both in the hallway but also in the classroom, the teacher asking for complete silence and then starting to shout all 150 students with full names), students coming in 20-40 minutes after the exam was supposed to start, the exam never started on time, you could ask questions during the exam, there were errors in exam papers, misleading information in the exam paper, poor lighting, easy to cheat if you wanted to (could go to the toilet unattended with your cell phone), 3 hours of assignments written by hand on paper and with a pen - the list goes on.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
There were large individual level differences between the different subjects. Some subjects were more simple, while others were informative to a level that seemed a bit excessive for a mere 6 ECTS. 

I had a course that consisted of dialect variations in Spain, not so much Spanish, but; Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Romance languages, Vasco, Gallego, Catalan, Caló, Turkish, Asturiano, Valenciano, Aragonés and all sub-dialects and idiosyncratic dialects. To make matters worse, the course contained 30-60 dialects and languages, which seemed a bit extreme for 6 ECTS. In País Vasco alone there were 9 major dialects (contemporary), in Aragon there were 5, etc. 
-all explained very quickly in class and no time for questions

Another course was very low key, where time was taken and there was time for questions. Both were worth 6 ECTS.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In Copenhagen, teacher and student are equal, the teacher may have more knowledge of the subject, but the hierarchy is no longer part of the teaching method. Unlike in Spain, the teachers stand on a podium, we speak in "Thus-form" (USTED) to them and when we need to ask a question, all the polite phrases are used. In addition, some teachers were people who stood in an auditorium and spoke without a microphone and without powerpoints. Other teachers used a microphone and/or powerpoints. At KU, almost all teachers use powerpoint or blackboard teaching, it's strange for me to imagine a teacher just standing in a corner mumbling something incomprehensible.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) An exchange program is not the same as improving your language, it's more about commitment and initiative, as well as a willingness to constantly keep speaking, in my case, Spanish and not switch to English, Catalan or Danish because it's easier. 

2) Spain is not Denmark, they do everything in a very different way. 

3) If you want to know something, your questions should be polite but at the same time concrete. In Denmark there is no word for "por favor", but there is in Spain and it's used a lot, as well as a lot of other phrases.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend a new student to take courses in places other than phonologia, in order to meet new people and teachers and get a better understanding of what it means to study and learn in Spain. 

I myself only chose phonologia because it was convenient that all the courses were in the same faculty, in retrospect I would probably have chosen differently if I could.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Finding out I could follow and participate in classes at a foreign university in a foreign language and without a safety net in the sense that I couldn't just say the sentence quickly as in Danish if I missed a verb.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting the right help as a dyslexic, it was difficult to convince the Spanish version of SPS that I had reading difficulties, because dyslexia does not exist in the same way in Spain as in Denmark.
